input:
Raoult's law provides a means of calculating the partial pressure of a component in an ideal liquid mixture from its liquid mole fraction and its pure-component vapour pressure at the temperature of the mixture, in accordance with the following relationship:

$$p = x P^*$$\n\nwhere $p$ represents the partial pressure of the volatile component, $x$ represents its liquid mole fraction, and $P^*$ represents its pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature. It is important to note that Raoult's law is based on the assumption of an ideal solution, and this assumption is stated here at the outset: no activity coefficients for the real mixture have been applied in this calculation. The mixture under consideration consists of ethanol in water, treated in an idealised manner, at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.3 for the volatile component, while the value of $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. Substituting these values into the relationship gives $p$ = 0.3 × 20.1 = 6.03 kPa, and the partial pressure is accordingly stated as 6 kPa. The partial pressure in question is the contribution made by the single component to the total pressure above the liquid, and it increases in direct proportion to the mole fraction, so that a richer liquid would yield a proportionally larger partial pressure at the same temperature. It should be emphasised, however, that the figure of 6 kPa which has been obtained is strictly an ideal-solution value: it applies to the mixture as idealised, at the mole fraction stated and at the temperature to which the pure-component vapour pressure relates, whereas a treatment of the real mixture would involve the application of activity coefficients and would produce a different partial pressure, and no activity-coefficient value has been stated or used in the present calculation.
